messages.author: d0d4a852dcbd9f5b
messages.subject: numerical problems after(?) warmup
parts:
I am trying to estimate individual risk aversion parameters from an experiment where participants choose between an uncertain lottery and a fixed amount of money. I use a typically assumed utility function where the utility of money is assumed to be a power function of money. I also have some scaling variables which are constrained to be positive by using the exponential transformation. That all the exponentiating and power function might not lead to the most stable numerical computations, so I was not too surprised when I got a bunch of warnings about numerical problems after warmup (with the experimental data and with simulated data) and divergent transitions (only with the experimental data). The divergent transitions are decreasing with higher adapt_delta but not disappearing entirely. The pairs plot shows them below the diagonal. 

I expected that the divergent transitions are related to my quick and dirty implementation and numerical issues. I tried to catch the numerical problems with print statements (see below). I got a lot of print statements at the start of warmup but none when Stan is sampling. (The warnings I get are always of the 'binomial_logit_log: Probability parameter[1] (the index varies) is nan (or inf) , but must be finite' variety). In one of my last tests, the last chain started after all the print statements and indeed that chain did not have any numerical warning. This lets me to believe that the warnings are actually not from numerical problems _after_ warmup but from _during_ warmup. Is that possible? That is actually my main question. 

If you have any tips or tricks for a better parameterization to avoid divergent transitions (or increasing stepsize?) I would be grateful. I am aware of some possible speed improvements but convergence and n_eff/second (2-3 for lp with the simulated data) is actually pretty decent so it's not my first priority.

You can find the R file for simulated data and the stan file attached.

Stijn


data{
  int<lower=1> Nchoices;
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> J;
  int<lower=0, upper=Nchoices> y[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=J> id[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=2> gain[N];
  vector[N] unc;
  vector[N] fixed;
  //vector[N] cond;
  vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] prob;
}

transformed data{
  vector[2] zeros;
  vector[N] absunc;
  vector[N] absfixed;
  zeros = rep_vector(0, 2);
  for (i in 1:N){
    absunc[i] = fabs(unc[i]);
    absfixed[i] = fabs(fixed[i]);
  }
}

parameters{
  row_vector<lower=0>[2] alpha0;
  real lambda0;
  real mu0;
  
  //vector<lower=0>[2] alphacond;
  //real<lower=0> lambdacond;
  //real<lower=0> mucond;
  
  row_vector<lower=0>[2] alphasd;
  real<lower=0> lambdasd;
  real<lower=0> musd;
  
  matrix[J, 2] alpha;
  vector[J] lambda;
  vector[J] mu;
   
  //cholesky_factor_corr[2] alphacorr;
}

transformed parameters{
}

model{
  matrix[J, 2] alpha_real;
  vector[J] mu_real;
  vector[J] lambda_real;
  vector[N] logisticy;
  
  //priors
  alpha0 ~ normal(.75, .5); //small average risk aversion
  lambda0 ~ normal(0, .5); // no loss overweighting. 
  mu0 ~ normal(0, 1);
  //alphacorr ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  
  alphasd ~ normal(0, 1);
  lambdasd ~ normal(0, 1);
  musd ~ normal(0, 1);
 
  to_vector(alpha) ~ normal(0, 1);
  lambda ~ normal(0, 1);
  mu ~ normal(0, 1);
  
  alpha_real = rep_matrix(alpha0, J) + alpha .* rep_matrix(alphasd, J); //uncorrelated
  mu_real = mu0 + musd * mu;
  lambda_real = lambda0 + lambdasd * lambda;
  
  for (i in 1:N){
    real lambda_temp;
    real LO;
    real SO;
    lambda_temp = gain[i] == 2 ? 1 : - exp(lambda_real[id[i]]);
    LO = lambda_temp * prob[i] * pow(absunc[i], alpha_real[id[i], gain[i]]);
    SO = lambda_temp * pow(absfixed[i], alpha_real[id[i], gain[i]]);
    logisticy[i] = exp(mu_real[id[i]]) * (LO - SO);
    if (is_nan(inv_logit(logisticy[i]))){
       print("nan:", LO, SO, mu_real[id[i]])
    };
    if (is_inf(inv_logit(logisticy[i]))){
       print("inf:", LO, SO, mu_real[id[i]])
    };
  }
  
  y ~ binomial_logit(Nchoices, logisticy);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] numerical problems after(?) warmup
parts:
Yes, it's possible to get numerical errors during warmup
when you're out in the tails of a model that go away
when you get to the typical set for sampling. We generally
only worry about the divergences and numerical issues after
warmup.

I don't know what the model is, but if you put fat uniform
priors, like uniform(0, 1000) on values, and declare <lower=0, upper=1000>
on the parameter, then the init is at 500 and can take you way
into the tails. Otherwise, you might able to to reduce the scale
of the init (from 2 down to 1, say) or work on non-centered parameterizations,
which convert variables into more unit scale variables where init
is more sensible.

- Bob

parts: Stan takes the

> On Oct 27, 2016, at 2:01 PM, stijn masschelein <stijnmas...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> - The problem is that Rstan reports the numerical problems as being after warm-up. I think they are from during warm-up.

If you could verify, then that's a bug that we need to get fixed! For
instance, if there's only one post-warmup iteration, do you get more than
one instance of the same warning reported?
> - Thanks for the init advice. That means that Stan takes the priors into account when setting the inits?

Not the priors, just the constraints. The inits are uniform(-2, 2) in
the unconstrained space to which the parameters are transformed.

So a positive-only parameter declared with <lower=0> is log-transformed
to the unconstrained space, where uniform(-2, 2) winds up producing results
non-uniformly in (exp(-2), exp(2)) after the exp transform back to the
constrained space. But an upper and lower-bound is done with a scaled
and translated logit, which puts the inits around the midpoint of the
constrained interval.

- Bob

It's a bug. I filed the report on github. https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/350

Not the priors, just the constraints.  The inits are uniform(-2, 2) in 
the unconstrained space to which the parameters are transformed

I quickly played around with the constraints. Setting them at some reasonable but improbable values helps a lot: less numerical problems and less divergent, quicker warmup and quicker convergence.

Stijn

On Thursday, October 27, 2016 at 5:30:24 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Stan takes the
> On Oct 27, 2016, at 2:01 PM, stijn masschelein <stijnmas...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> - The problem is that Rstan reports the numerical problems as being after warm-up. I think they are from during warm-up.

If you could verify, then that's a bug that we need to get fixed!  For
instance, if there's only one post-warmup iteration, do you get more than
one instance of the same warning reported?

> - Thanks for the init advice. That means that Stan takes the priors into account when setting the inits?

Not the priors, just the constraints.  The inits are uniform(-2, 2) in
the unconstrained space to which the parameters are transformed.

So a positive-only parameter declared with <lower=0> is log-transformed
to the unconstrained space, where uniform(-2, 2) winds up producing results
non-uniformly in (exp(-2), exp(2)) after the exp transform back to the
constrained space.  But an upper and lower-bound is done with a scaled
and translated logit, which puts the inits around the midpoint of the
constrained interval.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] numerical problems after(?) warmup
parts:
Thanks for filing the issue. We don't recommend big
constrained interval constraints for both statistical
and computational reasons. But whatever you do, you can
also provide inits to RStan for some or all of the parameters
and the rest will be initialized randomly.

- Bob
